narrative:
The model determined that you have a 57% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score of 25 was the strongest influence, pulling the prediction strongly toward failure. This score sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling that the model saw your test performance as a significant risk for not passing the bar.

Next, your first-year grades in law school ranked second. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) pushed the prediction further toward failure. In contrast, accepted students averaged around the 6th decile, so your early academic standing was viewed as much weaker than typical successful applicants.

Your third-year grades provided the only counter-balance, ranking third in importance. Being in the 4th decile nudged the prediction slightly toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your LSAT and first-year performance.

The model did not consider your gender, race, family income, or part-time status in reaching this decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation and building a stronger academic record if you retake courses. These two areas had the greatest influence on the outcome and are the most actionable for future applications. (248 words)
